planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil after danger of frost has passed.

directions: This West Virginia heirloom beefsteak produces huge pink, often heart-shaped fruits that can weigh a pound or more, with dense, juicy flesh and comparatively few seeds. The sweet, well-balanced flavor makes it a favorite for slicing, and the vigorous indeterminate vines perform especially well in hot, humid summers. Stake or cage plants and provide consistent moisture to limit cracking on the large fruits.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil has warmed.

directions: Named for the Ligurian coastal town of Albenga near Genoa, this ancient Italian heirloom bears deeply pleated, pear-shaped fruit that ripens pink to orange-red and can weigh well over a pound. The dense, juicy flesh has a mild, sweet flavor that Ligurian cooks traditionally favor for homemade sauce over San Marzano or Roma types. Being indeterminate, the vines need staking and benefit from even watering to fill out the pronounced ribbing without cracking.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil has warmed.

directions: This old Italian paste tomato, named for 19th-century King Umberto I, bears small elongated-oval fruits around 2-3 inches long with glossy deep-red skin and firm, low-juice, meaty flesh. Its rich flavor and sturdy texture suit whole canning, drying, and sauce-making, and the indeterminate plants crop reliably even in less than ideal conditions. A yellow-fruited sport, Re Umberto Giallo, is also grown, and historical accounts credit this variety as a parent of the San Marzano paste tomato.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this late-season variety benefits from an early start.

directions: This Virginia family heirloom produces massive pink beefsteak fruits, often 1-2 pounds, with a well-balanced, old-fashioned tomato flavor and subtle sweet undertones. It is a late-season, indeterminate variety, so gardeners in shorter-season climates should start seed early and provide sturdy staking to support the heavy fruit. Preserved through seed-saving networks, it has been noted for its resemblance to Radiator Charlie's Mortgage Lifter.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; this compact determinate variety does not need staking.

directions: Developed around 1915 by plant breeder Luther Burbank in Santa Rosa, California, this determinate heirloom yields heavy crops of medium-sized, round, deep-red fruit well suited to canning as well as fresh eating. The fruit resists cracking, and the compact plants tolerate drier conditions without staking, making this an easy-care choice for shorter growing seasons. Even watering and full sun give the most reliable yields.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; this compact bush type tolerates drier soil once established.

directions: A traditional tomato of Manduria in Puglia and a Slow Food Ark of Taste variety, this small, plum-shaped fruit has a slight pointed tip and hangs in grape-like clusters on compact, bushy determinate plants only 1-1.5 feet tall. Historically grown without irrigation in the dry soils of southeastern Italy, it tolerates heat and drought well once established and is used fresh, for passata, or dried. Its small stature also makes it a good candidate for containers and hanging baskets.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this rustic ecotype tolerates dry, saline soils once established.

directions: Grown for generations on the saline clay soils around Paceco in the Ericine Valleys near Trapani, Sicily, this rustic variety produces small, round red fruit with a distinctive pointed 'pizzo' tip at the blossom end, giving the variety its name. It is a Slow Food Presidium-recognized ecotype, traditionally raised without irrigation and prized for its sweetness fresh off the vine, in sauce, or hung in bunches to dry for winter use. The resilient plants show good tolerance of local pests and disease pressure.
